Some members laugh, but the department was right in this case. It was the form that was wrong. Regulation 201 covers the filing of these forms and states who must file them on dividends, interests and so on. It seems that in 1971 when the tax form went through, intentionally perhaps, the relieving provision which allows the person not to file the form for interest on loans from banks and other lending establishments disappeared. It would appear to me now that the government is checking this up and perhaps we will have a proper answer, hopefully from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) on this point. It appears that anyone who has borrowed money from a bank and does not issue the bank with a T-5 slip may be in breach of the tax law.
Speaking to the Canadian Tax Foundation, the former minister of national revenue, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), said that he was concerned about the tax law. He said that he considers tax reform as a continuing process and asked business to help keep the system in balance by continuing to press for changes in the law. Well, members of the House on my side, and certainly the taxpayers of Canada, want to see progress in this regard. The minister also apparently was in favour of a "softer" government attitude to ministerial discretion, technical amendments, and all demands for files and records.
We all know that the Department of National Revenue carries the big stick. If you do not obey the law and pay your tax, the department can do terrible things to you, that is, if you are still in Canada. Later we shall deal with what happens if you have left Canada. Apparently the minister was concerned about ministerial discretion and those powers in the area of tax law that allow the Department of National Revenue to decide whether a transaction is aimed at avoiding taxes.
As lawyers in this House know, a man should be entitled to so order his affairs as to minimize the incidence of taxation. It was the view of the department that it knew better, that it ought to decide this question, not the taxpayer, as if it were a crime to claim your rights under the law and reduce your taxes. I am sure that lawyers in this House, and taxpayers outside, will be delighted to note that the courts recently decided that a man still has the
Income Tax
right so to order his affairs as to minimize the incidence of taxation.
I hold in my hand another press clipping which illustrates the sort of thing that can happen when our so-called tax reform law fails. It is the hope of members on my side that, in addition to avoiding double taxation, the treaties we shall enter into with other countries will allow us to close certain tax loopholes. Just over one month ago the Financial Times reported that:
The government has shelved plans to close a 'tax loophole which costs the country hundreds of millions of dollars' ...
Why did the government decide to shelve those plans? Apparently Ottawa could not afford the extra investigators needed. This country employs 300,000 or 400,000 civil servants, depending on who counts them, and how the counting is done. It strikes me as odd that anyone should say we cannot afford a few expert investigators whose work may lead to the recovery of up to $2.7 billion. I think we heard that figure. At any rate the money lost to this country is enormous, and the work of the investigators would enable us to enforce collections against taxpayers who have left. The former minister of national revenue admitted that the loophole was costing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost revenue. He promised a series of proposals to "significantly strengthen Canada's compliance effort". I hope that this bill, and the treaties we expect will follow, will go some way to correct the difficulty.
Department of National Revenue spokesmen said that government austerity measures have put the investigation project "far down the road". I remind the House that an article written in November of last year dealing with tax dodgers and evasion outlined how the government was to attack this difficulty. According to the article appearing in the Globe and Mail of November 19, 1975:
A special task force on taxation has been set up by Canadian and U.S. authorities aimed at catching tax dodgers in both countries.
The force has been told to submit recommendations by the end of this year that may lead to a new Canadian-U.S. tax treaty,...
Canada's aim is to recoup an estimated $1.6 billion a year that is being lost through tax avoidance or fraud.
I think the minister denied that the figure was $1.6 billion. The article mentions the figure, but I will not insist on attributing it to the minister. Without doubt the minister was interviewed. According to the news report he said:
We want to see if we can do this through existing tax treaties ... If not, we may need a special agreement.
It remains to be seen what we shall do. If existing treaties are responsible for our present position, we may need to examine dozens more of these treaties.
As I wish to make some further comments, may I call it four o'clock?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON FRESHWATER AND INLAND FISHERIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Standing Orders of this House should be amended to provide that there shall be a Standing Committee on Freshwater and Inland Fisheries, distinct from the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, to which shall be exclusively referred all matters relating to the freshwater and inland fisheries of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak on this motion. The freshwater fishery of Canada is close to my heart and to the hearts of my constituents. The commercial, gill net freshwater fishery in many constituencies represents an important way of life. Freshwater fishing in Manitoba provides an important economic base and it is my concern that this valuable industry shall be kept alive and fishermen allowed the opportunity to remain in the freshwater fishing industry despite drawbacks-and believe me there are many-which have plagued them for years.
I am also concerned because freshwater fishermen are being short-changed because they do not receive from Ottawa the same recognition which coastal fisheries receive. I specifically refer to the present inability of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to deal adequately with the freshwater fishing industry. It is my conclusion that this standing committee does not-nay, cannot-spend enough time monitoring the workings of the freshwater fishery.
Today I shall propose to hon. members of this House that a separate committee be established to deal solely with the freshwater fishing industry of Canada. In doing so I have endeavoured to assimilate enough facts so that I can cogently present my ideas as to why a standing committee on freshwater and inland fisheries is desirable and, indeed, necessary.
First, let me review the history of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, the federal Crown corporation which, in effect, is the commercial freshwater fish marketing board in this country. I will then show how difficulties with the corporation and with the freshwater fishing industry in general have not been adequately dealt with in the respective standing committee of the House in the past.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Act was assented to on February 27, 1969, and came into force May 1, 1969, at which time the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was established for the purpose of marketing and trading
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. McCleave).]
in fish, fish products and by-products, in and out of Canada. The corporation has the exclusive right in interprovincial and export trade to market the products of the commercial fishery of the provinces participating in the program. The provinces, under Section 25 of the act, include the Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and western Ontario. As well, the object of the corporation is to increase returns to fishermen, promote markets, and increase inter-provincial and export trade.
The quality of the commercial freshwater fish that is regulated and handled by the corporation is comparable to any in Canada. Indeed Canada is unique in having a freshwater fishing industry that in many cases is the livelihood of hundreds of individuals and is the sole economic base of many regions.
Fishermen, however, have run into difficulties with their seasonal occupation since the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act was implemented in 1969. First of all-and this would especially apply to the province of Manitoba and in particular to my riding of Churchill-many fishing operations were disrupted as they were turned over to local co-operatives that would act as agents to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Fishermen were lost and some fishing was abandoned at this time because of alternative local job opportunities in the fields of farming, lumber, and logging, mechanics, carpentry, and general contracting, although hydro development in the north was a major controlling factor.
Many of the large commercial freshwater fish operations were out of production between 1972 and 1974. This was a crucial changeover period, the beginning of a regulated freshwater fishing industry that set the stage for a whole new area of responsibility for members of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
Then there was one of the most devastating examples of how fishermen in Manitoba and other member provinces were adversely affected by the actions of the corporation. I am talking now of the long standing strike at the freshwater fish marketing plant at Transcona, Manitoba. If members will recall, that strike began with a walkout of plant employees on October 11, 1974, after they had worked without a contract since March of that year. The strike that officially went into effect the following day ended with a new contract settlement five weeks later-after the near destruction of the freshwater fishery in Churchill constituency, and throughout the province the Transcona strike caused losses for fishermen who were not able to catch their quota before the strike began. This is unacceptable in light of the fact that the corporation was aware that its employees might eventually strike once their contract had expired. Yet no additional cold storage facilities were made available, and fishermen were ordered to pull up their nets and stop fishing.
These fishermen had virtually no one to go to bat for them. They had no federal body which they felt confident they could turn to, so many of them blamed the provincial government for inaction in regard to settlement of the strike. Had there been an exclusive freshwater and inland fisheries committee-or at least a special committee to which these fishermen could have presented their grievances-then the situation could have been different. The Fisheries and Forestry Standing Committee, as it is pres-
April 2, 1976

ently structured, is simply unable to monitor effectively the freshwater fishery.
There are other problems with which fishermen had had to contend. These are problems that fishermen themselves have brought to me, or that the co-operatives have tried to solve through resolutions-the majority of which, unfortunately, have fallen on deaf ears in the past. Not only has there been an over-all reduction in the number of fishermen, as I mentioned earlier, but there has been a marked decrease in the pounds of fish harvested. Fish not removed from lakes in the 1973-74 fishing season, for example, represented a total loss to the northern Manitoba economy of $2,123,336.
One of the most obvious reasons for this loss-and again, let me assure you there are many-is in the area of economics. Money lost through transportation costs represents by far the largest loss to fishermen. Rail and air transportation costs have risen to such an extent that freshwater fishermen in Manitoba are having a hard time absorbing costs. For example, air transportation from lake to railhead went up from $1.80 per ton mile to $3.20. Railways have doubled their freight rates. They have suggested that freight equalization be applied on the lake to rail, and rail or highway transportation.
The co-ops have also been faced with rising equipment costs. In fact these have doubled in the last few years. Wages for hired labour have increased from $300 per month to $600 per month. Even more shocking is the fact that, under present circumstances, fishermen are unable to dispose of their licences to heirs, successors, or to other fishermen. The average age of fishermen who fish Lake Winnipeg is 60 years of age. It is so difficult for young men to obtain operators' licences that many have given up fishing or have not even attempted to get a licence.
We know that the freshwater fish produced are of a high quality and are of a species readily marketed. Why then are fishermen dissatisfied with the way in which their operations are being handled, and why then do they think that a separate standing committee to deal with freshwater and inland fishing is so important to the success of their operations? A letter I received from the manager of Northern Co-operative Fisheries Limited best answers that question. The letter stated that:
.. . Generally speaking the fishermen, the agents, the corporation are trying to work on 100 cents on the dollar, while the actual cost is 125 cents on a dollar.
One paragraph of the letter effectively summed up the feelings of fishermen. It went like this:
I could almost assure you that it, lack of recognition, will destroy the Freshwater Fish Marketing Board within a year or two and I am saying this because the signs of erosion are all around us.
For example, the letter goes on to state:
The 1,400 fishermen belonging to 25 co-operatives and associations in the province of Saskatchewan have already delivered their ultimatum to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation that they will no longer deliver their fish in the traditional manner. Instead, they are asking the corporation to market their fish on a fee for service basis. Failing to accept this proposal, they will ask their minister ... to withdraw the commercial fisheries from the participating region of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Freshwater Fisheries
A resolution submitted to the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan and Manitoba Co-operatives Fisheries held in Prince Albert March 23, 24, and 25 of 1975 stated, and I will read this resolution in its entirety:
WHEREAS commercial fishermen in the Province of Saskatchewan and Manitoba are continuously experiencing difficulties in communication with the federal government,
AND WHEREAS the fishing operations are being complex and requiring assistance similar to the East and West Coastal Fisheries,
AND WHEREAS the present Parliamentary Fisheries Committee is made up of Eastern M.P.s who are not acquainted with the inland fisheries program,
BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Honourable Romeo LeBlanc, Minister of Fisheries, appoint an inland freshwater fish parliamentary committee to assist the freshwater fishing industry in their problems which lie within the jurisdiction of the Federal Committee.
This resolution refers to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Let me say that I first presented the idea to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry quite some time ago. In fact it was in 1974. I want to emphasize that again I am asking that consideration be given to this proposal.
I wish to refer to the resolution as submitted at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan and Manitoba Cooperatives Fisheries held in Prince Albert on March 23, 24 and 25 of 1976, just this past week. At that meeting there were representatives from all the major fisheries in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Northwest Territories, and Ontario. This is the resolution, and it is hoped there will be a more positive response to it:
WHEREAS the 1975 Resolution No. 10 requested that the Honourable Romeo LeBlanc, Minister of Fisheries, appoint an Inland Freshwater Fishery Parliamentary Standing Committee to assist with the problems relating to the Freshwater Fish Industry within the jurisdiction of the Federal Government.
WHEREAS, the Honourable Minister replied that there are three (3) Members on the Committee who represent the Freshwater Fisheries and that Quebec and New Brunswick also have a freshwater fishery and both Provinces have representation on this Committee.
THEREFORE, be it resolved that another request be made to the Honourable Minister of Fisheries pointing out the volume of the freshwater fishery production in other provinces, such as Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Northwest Territories and that he give his utmost consideration towards appointing a sitting Member from each of the above-mentioned Provinces and Territories to the proposed Standing Committee of Fisheries in the House of Commons.
The resolutions of 1975 and again of 1976 came from concerned fishermen. They did not come from agents and so forth. They came from people who are trying to make a living from commercial fishing in the freshwater fishing industry. In Manitoba a group of fishermen from north of the fifty-third parallel have formed the Northern Commercial Fishermen's Association. Fishermen throughout the north are becoming more and more concerned. They are not operating in a piecemeal manner. They are operating as a group, but they want to get a fair return for the effort they put into the fishing industry. They have been in it all their lives. At one time they could make a fairly reasonable living from fishing, but the high cost of transportation today seems to be the most important aspect of their problem. I ask the minister to consider very seriously having a separate committee to deal with the freshwater and inland fishery. That is a resource we have had for a long time, and it is renewable.

April 2, 1976
Freshwater Fisheries
We seem to spend an awful lot of time looking to the north for our energy resources, but we are not spending very much time considering the natural resources we have. In my opinion many of these natural resources are more important at the present time than much of the exploration work which is going on in the Arctic islands. I ask that every consideration be given to the immediate appointment of a separate committee to deal with this very complex problem and to help the fishermen solve this problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Alexandre Cyr (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON FRESHWATER AND INLAND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) requesting the appointment of another Standing Committee on Fisheries to which all matters concerning freshwater and inland fisheries in Canada will be referred.
The sponsor of this bill is a very active member of our Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forests. I do not wish to question the sincerity and the good intentions of the hon. member in presenting his motion, and without being an expert on the matter of fisheries, I believe that we are all sincerely working towards the improvement of the fishermen's lot and also to assist as much as possible fish processing plants, whether they are in the East, the West or even in the centre of Canada.
While I find many of the hon. member's arguments valid, I still cannot support this motion, since I believe that another standing committee of this House will not improve the freshwater and inland fisheries of Canada.
If my hon. friend is aware of the complexity of establishing committees in this House and the constant difficulty in having a quorum, he will realize it would be very difficult to find members to sit on that other committee.
As recorded in Hansard for March 31, 1976, this House has 20 standing and special committees, and six joint Senate and Commons committees. Most of these committees include 20 members. There are 30 members on each of the External Affairs, National Defence and Agriculture committees. Joint committees such as that of the Library of Parliament include 16 senators and 22 members of this House, 38 in all.
The hon. member for Churchill, quite coincidentally, sits on the same committees I am on, that is Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and also Fisheries and Forestry, where we also deal with environment. The hon. member is also on the Committee of National Resources and Public Works. It will be realized that when a member sits on three committees meeting at least twice a week, this means he has to attend at least eight to ten committee meetings each week.
Mr. Speaker, apparently the official opposition have some difficulty in making suggestions in this House. Apparently, that party lacks leadership and cannot agree on a particular matter. No doubt the hon. member for Churchill already discussed the proposals for a new committee on Freshwater and Inland Fisheries. He will have discussed it in caucus. But I doubt whether the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) agrees with him to

establish another standing committee of this House, because on October 28, 1975, if I remember correctly, the hon. member for Peace River, in a statement dealing with the Standing Orders, had this to say, and I quote:
... the government should introduce some flexibility in the control they are exercising on committee programs and chairing. Certain documents and reports tabled in this House should be automatically referred to committee, and certain committee reports such as that on public accounts for instance, should be debated in this House. Committees should be empowered to make inquiries when members feel they are needed. Committees should be reduced to a more limited size. Chairmen should be appointed in a more objective way, probably by a neutral source, and provision should be made for appealing the chairmen's decisions.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat these remarks by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin): "... committees should be reduced to a more limited size . .." This necessarily entails reducing the number of standing committees of this House, now totalling 30.
Mr. Speaker, why increase the number of committees when there are already too many. I believe that hon. members, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), would agree to reduce this number and have between 15 and 20 committees. Most members now sit on three or even four committees and it is difficult, indeed impossible, for a party like the New Democratic Party or the Social Credit Party to send a representative to each one of these committees.
That is why members of these parties, which have only 10 to 15 representatives in the House, are forced to run from one committee to another every day. For instance, in the fisheries and forestry committee on March 30, and the hon. member for Churchill could corroborate my statement, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt) arrived in the committee room at about 9:45 p.m. and as the Committee was to adjourn at ten o'clock he could not put his question. He was told that at the next sitting of the committee he would be the first to question witnesses. So the hon. member came to the committee and was recognized first to ask his question. It took from 15 to 20 minutes, then he had to leave for another committee of which he was also a member. Mr. Speaker, how is it possible for members who have to attend the debates of 4, 5 or 6 committees the same day to be really efficient and perform their tasks conscientiously? I say this is not possible.
Mr. Speaker, the committees or the House are always faced with the same problem; the governing party has to keep the quorum, so when the provisions of a bill are about to be adopted or when budgetary estimates are to be voted, the party whip as to run from one committee room to another and try to get the quorum. I wish we would have discussed a motion proposing to reduce the number of the standing committees of the House, and not to increase them.
In his motion, my good friend the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) requests that the new committee be responsible exclusively for the questions concerning freshwater and inland fisheries in Canada. This proposal might cause much discussion and bring about a constitutional debate with the provinces.
I shall ask a question to the hon. member, if he wants to answer it later: has he consulted his province concerning
April 2, 1976

his proposal that the federal government take exclusive control over freshwater and inland fisheries in his province? I can tell him that my province will not easily agree to let the federal government extend its responsibilities to the lakes and rivers of Quebec. It will be the same for the province of Ontario and for the other provinces, in the Prairies, in the Pacific or the Atlantic regions.
Mr. Speaker, in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, we have many very interesting sittings, since members from all provinces are most interested and our chairman, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) is doing a tremendous job, and I also ought to mention the cooperation of our vice-chairman, the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall). We discuss all problems, those of the Atlantic region as well as those of the Pacific, and those of the fisheries in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and those of the Great Lakes. We always have the cooperation of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Baker).
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could take fifteen, twenty or thirty minutes at the meetings of the committees on which I sit, particularly the committee of fisheries and forestry, to explain the requests of Quebec fishermen and the demands of processing plants owners; but it is impossible because every member must be given an opportunity to participate in the proceedings of the committee regardless of the area he represents. This is why in most committees the interventions of members are limited to fifteen minutes during the first round, then to ten minutes and finally to five minutes.
In Quebec, Mr. Speaker, and particularly in the Gaspe Peninsula, there are years when the fishing industry suffers ups and downs. As far as the fishing industry and particularly the salt and dried fish processing plants are concerned, the plant owners have had to face very serious problems these last few years.
In the Committee on Fisheries, I have taken the time that was allotted to me by the chairman to explain to the minister and his officials the sorry financial plight of Gaspe producers. Two representations convinced the minister to send his officials around the Gaspe Peninsula in order to make a field study and attempt to find a solution under existing regulations.
Recently, at a meeting of this committee, we considered the new policies on redfish quotas in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic Ocean. All members had enough time to express their views. I made several suggestions to the minister who will apparently take them under serious consideration when he drafts the new policies and establishes the redfish quotas for the years 1977 and 1978.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to underline the satisfaction we find in the Committee on Fisheries in working with the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), and I believe that all committee members share this view. I also want to emphasize the dedication of his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker). I have represented for many years in the House of Commons the beautiful riding of Gaspe and a group of citizens for whom I like to work, the fishermen. I must say that we have received a great deal from the central government. The work was not done so much in this House but rather in committee. I must also
Freshwater Fisheries
admit that we always had good people in charge of this department, both under the Pearson administration and under this government, under the direction and wise guidance of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not mention the dedication of the officials of the Department of Environment, in particular the Fisheries and Marine Service, who are really concerned about the problems of fishermen as regards freshwater as well as the Atlantic Ocean, in Nova Scotia, in Newfoundland or in British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, for the various reasons I have mentioned, I cannot support the motion of the hon. member for Churchill. Knowing how hard he tries to find more effective ways of helping fishermen, I am sure he will know how to convince them that his suggestion is not necessarily the best one.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a good experience to stand and support a motion presented by my colleague from Manitoba. speechtext: Ungracious!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS

speechtext:
It is known in the west that the inland fisheries are in trouble. There is a problem of great magnitude. In 1969 when the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was formed the catch in the province of Manitoba was 75 million pounds of fish. Last year, for the entire area covered by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, the catch was only 32 million pounds. Anyone from western Canada, anyone from any of the inland fisheries can tell you what the problem is.
If we want to understand the problems of the coastal fisheries we consult, for example, my colleague from South Shore. He can tell you about draggers, he can tell you about the continental shelf, he can tell you about the techniques which are used, he understands about Decca Loran and all the sophistication of electronic gear aboard modern trawlers. I can tell you that fishermen in my area, and in the area of which my colleague from Churchill speaks, have not even seen Decca Loran. My colleague from South Shore understands the problems of the coastal fisheries, but he does not pretend to know the problems of the inland fisheries or the solution to those problems.
It bothers me when we hear members opposite standing in their places as though they are the epitome of wisdom and pontificating upon solutions when they do not even know the problems. I can identify some problems very quickly for the benefit of members opposite. There are problems inherent within the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation itself. At the formation of that organization back in 1969 it was guaranteed by the then president that
12432

April 2, 1976
Freshwater Fisheries
they would handle every pound of fish for a cent or a cent and a half. We find, six or seven short years later, that one or one and a half cents has risen to 80 cents per pound. Between the time one pound of usable fish reaches the corporation and the time it leaves, 80 cents is gobbled up and lost forever to the fishermen.
As was stated by my colleague from Churchill, the objective of the marketing corporation when it was formed was to increase returns to the fishermen, not to build a conglomerate for the inland fisheries. That was not the purpose. Back in 1969 there was no talk of processing fish. It was to embody the concept of a one-desk marketing agency. For members opposite to stand up and maintain that everything is O.K. in the west and that if you understand fisheries, fisheries are fisheries anywhere in Canada, is to display ignorance of and a kind of indifference to what happens in western Canada.

speechtext:

Down in the maritimes when you want to build a processing plant, generally you build it by the wharf, by the water so that the ships can unload readily. That is the ordinary, common sense thing to do. But not the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Its building stands in the riding of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), right among the wheatfields! There stands this great modern fish processing plant, and the closest water anywhere is 55 miles away as the crow flies.
Hon. members opposite want to talk about nonsense. Mr. Speaker, they are the originators of nonsense when it comes to inland fisheries. Oh yes, and as always with this government, although the original cost was locked in, guaranteed, fixed at $3 million, by the time construction was finished, with the landscaping done and the flags flying in the cool breeze of western Manitoba, and the sun shining down, the balance sheet showed $5.5. million, almost double the original figure. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if that were the case all would be well. The people who paid were the very people this great corporation was established to help. It was the fishermen who paid. They paid for it, pound by pound, fish after fish.

speechtext:
They thought the fishermen were a bunch of mullets. And anyone knows, if he understands the fisheries, that the equivalent expression is "suckers". The fisherman in western Canada may only know about fishing, but they have more common sense in one little

finger than one can find on the whole of the treasury benches.
I could go on and talk about the effects of inflation which have hit the inland fisherman, just as they have affected coastal fishermen. I could talk about the problems of the quota system. Some fishermen in Manitoba particularly on Lake Winnipeg, are locked into the prices of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation quotas. The government says that they can catch no more fish at that price, period.
My hon. friends opposite can go on talking nonsense, but we have more important things to talk about in this motion of my colleague, which is not an unreasonable one. He simply wants a separate committee. He wants certain members of this Chamber who know something about the inland fishery to band together in a little group so that they do not waste the time of the existing committee on fisheries. He wants a little group of members of parliament from the west to form a committee to deal specifically and only with the inland fisheries. Though their numbers be few in western Canada, surely the fishermen of western Canada deserve no less than that.
In addition, I think the committee structure of the House ought to be reviewed in terms of numbers and the function of committees. The numbers are certainly too large in most cases. I am calling for a review of the committee structure and I am asking the government to think again. If hon. members opposite were to repent, fall to their knees, shed tears of true repentance, and say they have changed their minds, that on closer reflection and on more critical analysis they have decided to support our suggestion, I know my hon. friend from Churchill would accept it. I know he is not a vain man and that he would go back to the west and give the government its fair share of the credit for recognizing that there is a problem in western Canada that is unique, one that needs special and specific responses from the government.
The kind of response that is needed in western Canada is not exemplified by what happened a week ago today in the province of Manitoba when the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) denied the fishermen of Manitoba and the north the transportation subsidies they need to make their industry viable. These people were not talking about hundreds of millions of dollars, Mr. Speaker; they were not even talking about $1 million. They were talking about less than $1 million-the difference in transportation costs which would make the fisheries viable, that would make the difference between existing and not existing. This is the kind of sober second thought that my hon. friends opposite should give, instead of the kind of nonsense that has characterized the entire attitude of the government.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON FRESHWATER AND INLAND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I may say that I for one am proud to have the hon. member for Churchill as a colleague of mine. Coming specifically to the motion, I should like to respond to the view of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) that the committee structure at the present time is complex, that as members we have difficulty sitting on committees, that we do not review our work in committee sufficiently, and that we are not well enough prepared in committees. I accept those criticism and agree with them. But I wonder whether using that tack is not putting our finger on the difficulty we so often have as members in communicating with our constituents.
I am sure that all members of the House have had constituents come to them with a serious problem that can be solved, yet we come back to the Hill and become so wrapped in procedure and with making our little operation "efficient" that we lose sight of the very request that moved us to act in the first place. This is not unique to this government. I think it is in the nature of the thing, if I can put it in that way. So often we lose sight of the very real problems that people back home have. We say action cannot be taken for this reason or that. While efficiency might be sacrificed at times, the first job of all members is to respond to the needs of their constituents. To solve the problems they present to us is our obligation and is really, I suggest, the only reason for our existence.
The problem that concerns me about the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation is this. We know the corporation was established by joint agreement between the federal government and various provincial governments, in particular the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development through its responsibilities in the Northwest Territories. The way I understand the subsidy question at the present time-and the hon. member for Gaspe alluded to this-it is questionable whether the provinces would want the federal government to get involved in jurisdiction over the inland waterways, lakes, and so forth. Yet there is already an association in the minds of the fishermen, at least, that the federal government has become involved with the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation because of the very fact it has become operative.
I wonder whether here we are not discussing the same problem that I referred to earlier, and that is that the federal government has raised a constitutional question- rightly or wrongly I am not going to argue because I do not have the time. The fishermen are not concerned about constitutional problems. They are concerned about how they can retain a viable industry, one that has had real difficulty in the past. Efforts have been made by all parties
Freshwater Fisheries
to get the people who constitute this industry-their average age in Manitoba is over 60-to the point where they can retain their self-respect and earn their own income, so they can make their own way in life instead of constantly having to come to the government for subsidies.
I should just like to give a brief quotations from an article that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on Wednesday, March 31, as follows:
The federal minister turned the requests down on the basis that the federal government isn't responsible for inland fisheries.
There is the constitutional question that he raised.
"I was just incredulous. I couldn't believe his blunt statement disclaiming responsibility for inland fisheries," Mr. Bostrom said. "It puts northern fisheries in real jeopardy."
I am not quoting a Conservative, Mr. Speaker. I am quoting a constituent of mine who happens to be a minister in the present NDP government in Manitoba.
I should like to return to the motion of the hon. member for Churchill. He has made this suggestion. Surely members of good will can get together on this. If it turns out that a committee is not the right vehicle, let us develop some other structure. Surely through the House leaders we can take this step whereby a committee or subcommittee is formed to which a full time fisheries minister would report directly on inland fisheries. In this way members such as myself, who cannot sit on the other Standing committee on fisheries because of other responsibilities, could sit on that committee and represent the interests of our fishermen, for instance those along the eastern shores of Lake Winnipeg and in the northern parts of my riding. This is all the member is asking. I am sure hon. members opposite see his point of view.
Let us get together in that manner, with that kind of co-operation, in order to help those people who are asking for a minimum. This will give us a chance to help those who represent a very small number but are important to the well being of Canada. It is on that basis that I welcome the motion of the hon. member for Churchill and thank him for again making the House aware of the needs of these people.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' MOTIONS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDING COMMITTEE ON FRESHWATER AND INLAND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think today you are seeing in the House what happens in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and the Environment when a discussion on freshwater fishery comes to the fore. There you will see other hon. members back off and make room for the worthy gentleman, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), and for the somewhat histronic, at least today, hon. gentleman from Selkirk, and for the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). The committee always makes much room there for members who are inland fisheries oriented when it is time to discuss such important matters as the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
The hon. member for Churchill has requested that a special House committee be struck to deal exclusively with the concerns of freshwater fishing. I am sure the hon. member is just as sympathetic to the concerns of people on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts as we are to his. However, I
12434

April 2, 1976
Freshwater Fisheries
believe it would be really quite extraordinary for us to attempt to augment the already 26 House committees with yet another committee especially devoted to freshwater fish.
When I began to think of this, Mr. Speaker, I began to think of the number of specialized group in fisheries which could very well be served by a single committee within the House. I think of coastal surveillance, the coastguard, production marketing and research, small craft harbours, vessel subsidies and vessel contruction, and Environment Canada which, by the way, the hon. member for Proveneh-er will be interested to know, has responsibility for Northwest Territories fisheries.
Then we might also consider special species subcommittees. We would have one for lobsters, molusks, crustaceans and shellfish. We would have one for salmon, of course, the noble fish on the west coast, on which I am sure the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) would be glad to serve. We would have one for herring, groundfish, halibut, and all those other exotic Atlantic varieties.
We could then, of course, think of our friends at the Saltfish Corporation as well as the fish oil producers. We could have a special committee for some of those marine menaces of which we have an abundance on the west coast, and which represent a very serious problem to our fisheries. I have in mind the dogfish which load down the gill nets to such a degree that the fishermen must cut their corklines allowing their $3,000 lines to sink, because there is just nothing they can do about the dogfish.
Then there are those other menaces of the sea such as the lamprey, the harbour seals, and scavangers of all kinds which would have to be the subject of special committees. We could have a committee for the smoked saltwater and smoked freshwater fish, both varieties pickled, and all kinds canned. Then there are the meal producers who, of course, would want to be part and parcel of any special committee we would strike.
I believe all of these things are valuable and many of them have been the subject of discussion by the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry. In fact this infinite variety of concern has been the matter of discussion at the standing committee. I have seen that committee deal with the whole spectrum from seal pups to pipeline threats to salmon smolts; from spawning grounds and ultra high frequency communications between vessels to everything else. This is an everyday occurrence at that vital committee.
Members opposite have played a very active role on that committee. Indeed I would say it is one of the least partisan committees on which I have had the privilege of serving since coming here. The present system is not perfect, but to single out one area of importance equal to at least ten others for a special committee is simply impossible and impractical. The 26 committees of the House would be augmented on fisheries concerns alone by 56
committees, and they in turn would have to be augmented ad infinitum. I might say that even with the committees we now have it is often difficult to get a quorum, in spite of the ambitious members on the other side.
It is interesting to note that the attendance at the committee dealing with the environment was very large the other day, but when fisheries came up for discussion the other night members opposite were indeed few to be found. It is interesting to note also that when we have a discussion on a question of very great importance to those hon. members, the members on our side back off, as I said in the beginning, and refuse to enter into the discussion so that more questions can be put in respect of those areas where we indeed lack expertise.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) does not have to tell me that I do not know what kind of fish swim in the water in his part of the country, but then again he does not know the difference between a troller and a trawler. However, that makes no difference to me. There are many places where co-operation, not partisanship, shines forth, and one such place is the present standing committee.
This is a government which has shown a concern unmatched by any previous administration in its positive actions on behalf of fishermen. The painstaking debate in New York on the extension of the 200 mile limit at the Law of the Sea Conference is but one example of the devotion and expertise that the Minister of State for Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) brings to his task.
There are fisheries enhancement programs in British Columbia. There are programs in respect of safety at sea. This has seen changed in surveillance and tracking and rescue techniques. This will result in greater search and rescue ability in this country, and this is the value of the new policy forthcoming on search and rescue.
There is also the Indian fishermen's assistance program whereby native fishermen can make their way into a business they once dominated. I like to think, as a native Indian in my part of the country always says, they are not using anything that is theirs when they are taking the salmon but rather they are taking their grandchildren's salmon. I should like to think that this committee would not become so specialized that I cannot take as much interest in the legacy of the grandchildren of the hon. member for Churchill as he does in the legacy of my own grandchildren. Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock.
